articles.title: llm 0.37
articles.summary: Release: llm 0.37 There's a lot of stuff in this new release of my LLM CLI tool and Python library, representing around two months of accumulated features and fixes. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra, plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna. LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2, which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. articles.title: What actually broke when I tried to fine-tune on web-scraped data and what fixed it [D]
articles.summary: Fine tuning on self collected web data felt straightforward until it wasn’t. Here’s what actually caused problems: Boilerplate contamination was the silent killer. Navigation menus, cookie banners, and footer text were leaking into training examples. The model started generating weirdly structured outputs that looked like half-rendered HTML. Solved it with aggressive DOM-targeting rather than raw text extraction and switching to a rotating residential proxy layer (per-request IP rotation means target sites serve you the same rendered DOM a real browser session would get, rather than a bot-filtered skeleton) made a noticeable difference in how clean the raw HTML was before I even touched the parser. Deduplication order mattered more than I expected. Running exact dedup before fuzzy dedup produced meaningfully different training sets than the reverse. articles.title: RoboArchitect: Automating the Design of Robotic Agents with Persistent Memory
articles.summary: Recent work shows that a frozen robot policy performs far better inside an agent harness, where control code decides when to query the policy, consult vision tools, or command the arm directly. Yet today these harnesses are built by hand and redesigned for each new robot or benchmark. We show that harness design can be automated, offering a strong alternative to finetuning on a novel setup. In RoboArchitect, a coding model observes a robot's rollouts, diagnoses failures, and iteratively revises the harness around the frozen policy. The harness evolves on a set of episodes for its optimization and is evaluated on held-out scenes and tasks. Without updating any model weights, RoboArchitect raises average success from 9.7% to 43.3% on unseen scenes (4.5x) and from 12.7% to 40.2% on unseen tasks (3.2x), across multiple benchmarks and policies. articles.title: We have access to the most powerful AI in history, yet I sometimes have absolutely no idea what to do with it. Is that a lack of imagination?
articles.summary: This has been bothering me lately. I use AI extensively for software development, work, research, and everyday tasks. Tools like Claude, Codex, and GPT have become part of my daily routine. They've made me significantly more productive. But here's the weird part. Sometimes I finish everything I need to do, and I still have plenty of tokens, usage limits, and access to incredibly powerful models. And I just sit there thinking... now what? I literally have access to something resembling a team of brilliant engineers, researchers, and problem solvers, available almost 24/7. I could build something, explore some crazy idea, experiment with things that would've been impossible for a single person just a few years ago. But I can't think of anything particularly exciting to do with it. Meanwhile, I see people creating incredible things with the exact same tools. And it makes me question myself.
